item.title: Drop-in Vintage CPU Replacements with the tranZPUter Project
item.description: Breathing new life into vintage hardware using modern microcontrollers like the RP2350B and clever PIO peripherals is pure hacker craft. It's a fascinating look at keeping rare 8-bit and 16-bit systems alive when original silicon gives up the ghost.
item.content:encoded:
from the retro-fitting silicon dept.

Breathing new life into vintage hardware using modern microcontrollers like the RP2350B and clever PIO peripherals is pure hacker craft. It's a fascinating look at keeping rare 8-bit and 16-bit systems alive when original silicon gives up the ghost.

The tranZPUter project uses modern FPGAs and MCUs to create drop-in replacement CPUs for vintage systems like those based on the Motorola 6809 and Z80. By leveraging the PIO peripherals of the RP2350B, makers can bypass unobtanium parts and keep classic computers running.

Read it · DotNet and Development · Hackaday

item.title: Chandra Unmasks Outbursts from a Massive Star
item.description: Understanding the erratic behavior of hyper-massive stars 30 million light-years away gives astrophysicists a front-row seat to stellar instability. NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory continues to unpack what makes these volatile giants tick.
item.content:encoded:
from the high-energy astrophysics dept.

Understanding the erratic behavior of hyper-massive stars 30 million light-years away gives astrophysicists a front-row seat to stellar instability. NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory continues to unpack what makes these volatile giants tick.

Using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have uncovered what triggers repeated, violent outbursts from AT 2016blu, an unstable star at least 33 times the mass of our Sun located in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559.

Read it · Astronomy and Space · NASA News

item.title: Shape-Shifting Robotic Slugs Inspired by Tensegrity Architecture
item.description: Traditional wheeled rovers struggle with jagged planetary boulders and tight crevices, making alternative morphologies essential for future exploration. Borrowing structural design principles from architecture could give future space probes a completely new way to navigate alien worlds.
item.content:encoded:
from the extraterrestrial crawling dept.

Traditional wheeled rovers struggle with jagged planetary boulders and tight crevices, making alternative morphologies essential for future exploration. Borrowing structural design principles from architecture could give future space probes a completely new way to navigate alien worlds.

Researchers at Colorado State University's Adaptive Robotics Lab have described a shape-shifting robot morphology based on tensegrity—a principle usually seen in architecture—designed to help rovers traverse difficult extraterrestrial terrain.

item.title: Asteroid Bennu Samples Deliver Fresh Prebiotic Surprises
item.description: Comparing asteroid return samples with known meteorites using atomic-level isotope techniques gives researchers a sharper window into the early solar system. It is a fantastic look at how organic precursors to life formed across different parts of the protoplanetary disk.
item.content:encoded:
from the organic origins dept.

Comparing asteroid return samples with known meteorites using atomic-level isotope techniques gives researchers a sharper window into the early solar system. It is a fantastic look at how organic precursors to life formed across different parts of the protoplanetary disk.

Researchers analyzing samples from asteroid Bennu alongside the Murchison meteorite have measured individual atomic isotope differences within the amino acid beta-alanine. The results indicate that some prebiotic building blocks formed under varying conditions in the early solar system.

Read it · Astronomy and Space · Universe Today

item.title: Chandra Unmasks a Supernova Impostor
item.description: Distinguishing between cataclysmic stellar deaths and recurring outbursts from unstable massive stars is notoriously difficult. Finding a compact binary companion behind the outbursts solves a long-standing astronomical mystery.
item.content:encoded:
from the cosmic masquerade dept.

Distinguishing between cataclysmic stellar deaths and recurring outbursts from unstable massive stars is notoriously difficult. Finding a compact binary companion behind the outbursts solves a long-standing astronomical mystery.

New research using the Chandra X-Ray Observatory reveals that a periodic 'supernova impostor' star outburst is actually powered by a binary relationship with a black hole or neutron star. Luminous Blue Variables often mimic true supernovae, but their recurring flares point to complex stellar interactions.

Read it · Astronomy and Space · Universe Today

item.title: What Happens When Asteroid Mining Hits the Market?
item.description: Discussions of space mining usually focus on the rocketry and engineering rather than the macroeconomic reality. Applying system dynamics to platinum market shocks provides a grounded look at future space industry economics.
item.content:encoded:
from the extraterrestrial commodities dept.

Discussions of space mining usually focus on the rocketry and engineering rather than the macroeconomic reality. Applying system dynamics to platinum market shocks provides a grounded look at future space industry economics.

A pair of system dynamicists from MIT have modeled the economic impact of harvesting platinum-group metals from asteroids using spacecraft like AstroForge. Their research suggests that while asteroid mining would crash rare-earth commodity prices, the broader industrial availability would benefit Earth immensely.

Read it · Astronomy and Space · Universe Today

item.title: The Ice Giants' Strange and Shifting Magnetic Fields
item.description: Uranus and Neptune have long puzzled astronomers with magnetic fields that bear little resemblance to Earth's orderly dipole. New modeling suggests these chaotic fields may change on surprisingly short timescales compared to our last visit from Voyager 2. It is a fascinating look at the dynamic interiors of the solar system's ice giants.
item.content:encoded:
from the planetary dynamo dept.

Uranus and Neptune have long puzzled astronomers with magnetic fields that bear little resemblance to Earth's orderly dipole. New modeling suggests these chaotic fields may change on surprisingly short timescales compared to our last visit from Voyager 2. It is a fascinating look at the dynamic interiors of the solar system's ice giants.

New research suggests that the messy, tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may change on very short timescales, potentially looking quite different than they did during Voyager 2's flybys in the 1980s. These findings highlight how little we still know about the unique interiors of our solar system's ice giants.

Read it · Astronomy and Space · Universe Today

item.content:encoded:
